children: Renesas India President Malini Narayanamoorthi says the company is moving beyond an engineering base to build products by India, for India, in India, while deepening its semiconductor manufacturing footprint

Renesas Electronics is expanding its India operations beyond engineering and research, with the Japanese semiconductor maker crossing 1,000 employees in the country and building capabilities across chip and system design, software development and semiconductor packaging and testing.

The company has added a second facility in Bangalore, opened a research and development (R&D) facility in Hyderabad, a location in Noida and plans to open a facility in Pune by December, as it seeks to develop products specifically for the Indian market, Malini Narayanamoorthi, President of Renesas Electronics India and Vice President at Renesas Electronics, told BW Businessworld on the sidelines of Electronica India.
“The vision is to build products by India, for India, in India,” Narayanamoorthi said, describing the expanded role of India within Renesas’ global operations.
Renesas had previously set a target of reaching 1,000 employees in India. It has now crossed that mark and expects to continue expanding, Narayanamoorthi said.

The expansion is also changing the nature of work being undertaken in the country. An important portion of Renesas’ 3-nanometre chip development is being carried out in Noida, while system design for 3-nanometre chips is being undertaken in Bangalore, she said.
The Hyderabad operations include R&D and laboratories, with a focus on areas including automotive compute, while Pune is being developed as an automotive and system-design hub.

The company’s India operations are increasingly involved in complete product journeys rather than isolated engineering functions, with the aim of developing products suited to India’s specific applications and requirements as well.
“Our scaling in India continues. It’s a fairly continuous process and the growth isn’t stopping,” Narayanamoorthi added.
Design To Manufacturing
The expansion on the design side is being matched by a push into semiconductor manufacturing and backend operations.

CG Semi, the joint venture between CG Power and Industrial Solutions, Renesas and Thailand's Stars Microelectronics, began commercial production at its G1 outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) facility in Sanand, Gujarat, in July.

The facility has a peak capacity of up to 300 million units a year and has completed equipment installation, process stabilisation, workforce training, customer qualification and quality-readiness processes. The wider joint venture is investing more than Rs 7,600 crore over five years across its facilities.

The first commercial shipment from the Sanand facility was sent to Renesas customers in Malaysia, linking the new Indian backend operation to the Japanese company’s global supply chain. CG Power has an offtake agreement with Renesas covering around 40-50 per cent of the facility’s output, according to recent industry reporting.

The facility is eventually expected to scale towards 15 million units a day, according to the partners’ plans. Renesas has said the joint venture is intended to strengthen India’s semiconductor ecosystem while combining CG Power’s manufacturing capabilities with Renesas’ semiconductor technology and Stars Microelectronics’ OSAT expertise.
For Renesas India, the facility could become an increasingly important part of the company’s localisation strategy.

“If you really want to localise product built in India, you need many pieces in the puzzle,” Narayanamoorthi said, pointing to the sequence from architecture and design to fabrication, packaging, assembly and testing.
Renesas is the anchor customer for the CG Semi facility and intends to support the operation as it scales, she said.
“Products that we try and design in India, we’ll want to work with CG Semi so that we can get more and more done in India,” she said.
The development is a shift from building engineering capacity in India towards connecting local design and product development with a domestic semiconductor backend ecosystem.

Renesas’ expansion comes as India’s semiconductor policy moves beyond attracting fabrication and packaging investments towards developing a broader ecosystem covering chip design, materials, equipment, research and talent. The government’s second phase of its semiconductor programme, ISM 2.0, has an outlay of about Rs 1.27 lakh crore, compared with Rs 76,000 crore under the first phase (ISM 1.0). The broader programme is intended to support capabilities across the semiconductor value chain.
For Renesas, the opportunity is increasingly to connect those layers.
AI Changes The Product Equation
Renesas is also expanding the software component of its India operations as semiconductor products become increasingly tied to AI and software.

India’s software talent pool is being leveraged for Renesas 365, a platform that brings hardware and software together to simplify product development. Narayanamoorthi said this could help Indian startups and smaller companies, including MSMEs reduce design complexity and improve time to market.
Narayanamoorthi also sees AI as an area where localisation will become increasingly important.
“The point of AI and AGI is to take your daily electronics and add intelligence to it,” she said, adding that such intelligence would eventually need to be adapted to local requirements.

In automotive, Renesas is seeing the industry move towards software-defined vehicles (SDVs), although Narayanamoorthi said India was still in the process of bringing together the different components required for the transition.
Focus On Engineering Talent
The increasing lean towards AI and integrated semiconductor systems is also changing the skills Renesas requires.
Narayanamoorthi said system-design capabilities would become increasingly important as AI is integrated deeper into semiconductor products.
“If they’re siloed, you might design something from an AI standpoint, it may not work at an SoC standpoint,” she said.
The company is also working to expand the semiconductor talent pipeline through the government-backed Chips to Startup (C2S) programme.

The programme now covers more than 300 colleges and universities, while Renesas has expanded from an initial engagement with IIT Hyderabad to deploying curriculum, kits and PCB design and layout programmes across more than 100 institutions this year, Narayanamoorthi said.
The kits include microcontrollers, connectivity components, power components and sensors, allowing students to develop applications rather than focus only on individual components.
Narayanamoorthi said engineering education should also place greater emphasis on product thinking, go-to-market skills and technical communication.
“There’s a big delta between creating a product and then actually monetising it effectively,” she said.
